arxiv-2605-08763: A single language model probing a network is a nuisance; several cooperating models could become a genuine threat. Minfeng Qi and five coauthors sketch a framework in which multiple LLMs team up to carry out automated cyber intrusions, splitting the attacker's work across specialized roles. The 2026 paper is defensive security research: it maps the threat so defenders can prepare for it.
arxiv-2605-08863: Multiple instance learning labels whole bags of examples — a medical scan counts as sick if any patch is — and max-pooling networks pick the loudest patch. Shota Fujikawa and Issei Sato revisit the design, analyzing the role of semantic probability in how the pooling decides. The 2026 paper is a careful re-examination of a workhorse architecture.
arxiv-2605-08963: Health surveys never sample the population evenly — the sick, the poor, the remote get missed — and naive machine learning bakes in that bias. YongKyung Oh, Henry W. Zheng, Jeffrey Feng, and Alex A. T. Bui offer a scoping-review-based guideline for survey-aware machine learning, keeping population-health inferences valid. The 2026 paper is methodology for honest public-health AI.
arxiv-2605-09063: Most math benchmarks test homework problems; research-level mathematics is another beast entirely. Soohak is a mathematician-curated benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can do research-level math. The 2026 paper sets a harder bar: problems chosen by working mathematicians, not scraped from textbooks.
arxiv-2605-09163: AI agents granted too many permissions — over-privilege — are accidents waiting to happen. Shawn Li, Chenxiao Yu, Han Wang, and colleagues introduce FORTIS, a benchmark for over-privilege in agent skills. The 2026 paper measures whether agents reach for powers they should not have.
arxiv-2605-09363: Game-playing algorithms usually guarantee average performance, but the last iterate — the final strategy — is what you deploy. Soumita Hait, Ping Li, Haipeng Luo, and Mengxiao Zhang prove near-optimal last-iterate convergence for zero-sum games with bandit feedback and opponent actions. The 2026 paper is game theory with deployable guarantees.
arxiv-2605-09463: Long-context models compress what they read, and position bias — favoring the start and end — corrupts the compression. Jiwei Tang, Zhijing Huang, Xinyu Zhang, and colleagues shift from position-driven to semantic-driven compression. The 2026 paper makes models remember what matters, not just what is recent.
arxiv-2605-09663: Classifiers decay as the world drifts beneath them; testing robustness demands realistic drift simulation. Julien Lafrance, Richard Khoury, and Véronique Tremblay build a digital twin framework driven by causal parametric drift. The 2026 paper stress-tests classifiers against the world of tomorrow.
arxiv-2605-09763: Thompson-like groups keep yielding surprises, and the Belk-Hyde-Matucci group V_A is a recent addition to the zoo. José Burillo and Marc Felipe study its cyclic subgroups in detail. The 2026 paper is geometric group theory on a fresh and fascinating object.
arxiv-2605-09863: Production LLM agents drift in persona — subtly becoming someone else over weeks of deployment. Chunxiao Wang detects that drift black-box with Nautilus Compass. The 2026 paper is essential production AI monitoring for identity drift. It tirelessly watches the watchers now.
plos-pone-0003463: Cancer geneticists measured mutation hotspots in this 2008 cell study. In cells with broken DNA mismatch repair, the repetitive coding stretches of two tumor-suppressor genes, TGFBR2 and ACVR2, mutate at high rates, driving colon tumors. By clocking those mutation rates directly, the team quantified a key step in microsatellite-unstable cancers.
plos-pone-0003563: Plant biologists caught a key relay in blue-light sensing in this 2008 paper. Cryptochrome 1 detects blue light to steer development, and the team showed the protein HFR1 is crucial for the early wave of gene changes that follow. Without HFR1, the plant's first response to blue light falls apart at the transcriptome level.
plos-pone-0003663: In 2008, a team tested hand-eye links in Parkinson disease. Patients showed clear gaps in turning what the eyes see into guided movement. The gaps point to where the illness breaks the chain between seeing and doing.
plos-pone-0003763: Larsen, Xu, and Cermelli found the traffic cop for fat droplets in this 2008 paper. The protein BicaudalD actively tunes microtubule motor activity during lipid droplet transport. The regulation shows how cells steer their fat cargo with precision along molecular highways.
plos-pone-0003863: In 2008, a team read nicotine's chemical signature in blood. Profiling 198 metabolites in 283 human serum samples, Wang-Sattler and colleagues linked smoking to distinct metabolic shifts. The first results show how deeply nicotine rewires the body's chemistry.
plos-pone-0003963: In 2008, Zhang, Chen, and Niewiadomska mapped HIV's counterattack on cellular defenders. Distinct spots on HIV-1 Vif and human APOBEC3 proteins proved needed to suppress diverse viral strains. The determinant map charts the arms race at the molecular level.
plos-pone-0004063: In 2008, Mamiya, Beshel, and Xu mapped how flies feel the wind. Mushroom body neurons in Drosophila responded to airflow patterns. The higher brain center, known for smell, also tracks air movement. The neat finding widens the mushroom body's sensory role.
plos-pone-0004163: In 2009, Stolze-Rybczynski, Cui, and Stevens studied fungal catapults closely. Spore discharge in Basidiomycota rides on Buller's drop, a racing fluid droplet still. The team compared the launch gear across many species. The neat physics reveals evolution tuning a micro-catapult.
plos-pone-0004263: In 2009, Gross, Pahl, and Si found bees doing math with their eyes. Honeybees generalized visual patterns by sheer number. The insects matched quantities across new images. The neat feat shows numerical skill beyond vertebrates. The tiny brains handled abstract quantity.
plos-pone-0004363: In 2009, Gupta, Ho, and Ha found a deacetylase moonlighting as a protein chaperone. HDAC3 shuttled phosphorylated TR2 to PML bodies. The chaperone job needed no deacetylase activity. The finding rewrites HDAC3's resume. The novel role matters for stem cell biology.
plos-pone-0344063: Spiders are nocturnal hunters — but do they run on an internal clock like humans do? This study exposed spiders to light at different times and read their gene activity to find out. The team mapped the spiders’ light-sensitivity rhythm and pinpointed candidate genes behind their daily clock, new evidence that even spiders keep time.
plos-pone-0353063: Mouflons — wild sheep of the Mediterranean — need the right habitat to thrive, and conservationists need maps of where that is. This paper compared two approaches to habitat suitability assessment: expert judgment versus species distribution models. The head-to-head test shows which method pinpoints mouflon territory more reliably.
plos-pone-0358863: Computer models of the human body need accurate joints to predict movement and injury. This paper updated the articular — joint-surface — representation of the TLEM 2.0 musculoskeletal model. The refined geometry makes the widely used leg model more faithful to real anatomy.
plos-pone-0352763: Car brake fluid is harsh chemistry, and plastic parts must survive it. This paper investigated crack initiation and mechanical behavior of polypropylene and polymer composites deforming in automotive brake fluid. The findings tell materials engineers which plastics hold up — and where cracks begin.
plos-pone-0358263: Research on older adults living with HIV works better when they help design it. This scoping review examined the role of co-design and co-creation methods in research supporting this group. The synthesis shows how involving patients as genuine partners improves both the science itself and whether its findings get used.
plos-pone-0358363: Startups drown in data but starve for insight. This paper tested how big data capabilities and business model innovation together impact new venture performance. The combined effect shows that data only pays off when the business model knows what to do with it — technology and strategy must move as one.
plos-pone-0358463: Buildings chase air temperature — but operative temperature, what bodies actually feel, is the real target. This paper examined leveraging operative temperature space to discover bioinspired thermal design features. The nature-inspired features promise human comfort with less energy spent on heating and cooling.
plos-pone-0357963: A lung nodule on a scan poses the dreaded question: harmless or cancer? This paper built multi-view attention-based deep learning for benign–malignant classification of pulmonary nodules. The model helps radiologists sort the worrisome nodules from the benign ones with greater confidence.
plos-pone-0357463: Predicting court judgments with AI is legal tech’s grand promise — and its hardest problem. This paper proposed legal judgment prediction via dynamic task graphs and keyword-aware contrastive learning. The architecture reads cases structurally, the way lawyers do, rather than treating law as mere text.
plos-pone-0354463: How common is treated glaucoma in Britain — and is it rising? This paper tracked the incidence rates and prevalence of treated glaucoma in the United Kingdom from 2000 to 2022. The twenty-two-year trends give eye-care planners the long view they need.
plos-pone-0356563: Tourism reshapes even the viruses circulating in a region. This paper tracked the dynamic changes of HPV genotypes in a tourism-influenced populated area of northeastern Iran. The shifting genotype patterns inform vaccination strategy where visitor flows mix populations.
plos-pone-0356063: Fear leaves a chemical signature in dogs’ blood. This targeted lipidomics study found altered serum phosphatidylcholine levels in fearful dogs compared to calm ones. The lipid changes mark canine anxiety objectively — a potential blood test for an invisible suffering.
plos-pone-0356463: Fixed point theorems quietly solve boundary value problems across science and engineering. plos-pone-0357263: Traffic police can’t be everywhere — so districting and patrol routes must be optimal. This paper proposed resilience enhancement-oriented service district division and patrol route planning. The optimization keeps cities covered even when the network is stressed.
plos-pone-0355963: The New World screwworm — a flesh-eating livestock parasite — demands ruthless, efficient control. This paper built a mathematical model for that efficient control. The equations tell eradication programs exactly where to strike, when, and how hard.
plos-pone-0356763: In second-hand markets, photos sell — but whose photos work best? This paper compared user-generated, firm-generated, and mixed photos across price conditions, measuring visual sources and information usefulness. The findings tell resellers exactly which imagery moves goods at which price points.
plos-pone-0355863: Jellyfish can regenerate lost body parts — and their microbiomes may be calling the shots. This paper investigated microbiome modulation in jellyfish regeneration. The findings add a surprising microbial dimension to one of nature’s most remarkable healing abilities.
plos-pone-0356263: Breast cancer risk assessment could save lives — but will underserved women accept it? This paper explored acceptability among women aged 30–49 from six under-served groups. plos-pone-0356363: Highway slopes in alpine regions are fragile ecosystems. This paper studied how soil aggregate size relates to electrical conductivity, organic carbon, and nutrient availability on these slopes. The soil science guides engineers building roads that don’t trigger erosion and ecological collapse in thin mountain air.
plos-pone-0355463: Reliability engineers need inference methods that handle complex censoring. This paper developed classical and Bayesian reliability inference for the Chen distribution under a block-adaptive progressive hybrid censoring plan. The statistical advances give engineers trustworthy tools for predicting product lifetimes from incomplete data.
plos-pone-0348463: Neem extract — a botanical pesticide — affects non-target brine shrimp in complex ways. This paper combined high-throughput transcriptomics with phenotypic analysis to study its effects on Artemia franciscana. The findings reveal the molecular footprint of a ‘natural’ pesticide on aquatic life.
plos-pone-0355563: Young Camogie players asked to ‘play up’ an age grade face unique pressures. This qualitative study examined their perceptions of the experience. plos-pone-0354363: Increased nuchal translucency — fluid at the fetal neck — raises anxious questions. This paper examined the molecular genetic and pregnancy outcomes of affected fetuses. The findings give expectant parents and their doctors the prognostic data that screening results demand.
plos-pone-0355163: Open science — sharing data, code, and methods — needs support at scale. This paper examined supporting open science practices across multidisciplinary scales. The findings map what institutions must do to make openness the default rather than the exception.
plos-pone-0354663: Social media drives adolescent risk behaviors in North India — and social marketing might counter it. europmc-pmc2802563: Back in 2009, when social media was still young, this paper examined how Americans were using it and what that meant for health communication. europmc-pmc2857863: The brown dog tick spreads disease to dogs and people across warm lands. This 2010 paper reviews its biology and ecology, from life cycle to habits. The author gathers what tick fighters need to know. The review is a one-stop reference for a pest of global reach.
europmc-pmc2895663: Two germs attack the worm C. elegans in different ways. This 2010 paper compares the distinct pathogenesis and host responses during infection by P. aeruginosa and S. aureus. europmc-pmc2898863: Air pollution kills millions, but measuring it worldwide is hard. This 2010 paper estimates fine particle levels across the globe from satellite views of haze. europmc-pmc2909263: Cholesterol shards do more than clog pipes; they light fires. This 2010 paper shows the shards trip an alarm, the NLRP3 inflammasome, in human guard cells. The authors tie cholesterol handling to body inflammation. Their find helps tell why fatty arteries burn.
europmc-pmc2972763: Rotavirus killed countless children, and this 2003 paper counts them. The authors estimate global illness and deaths from rotavirus disease in children. Their tally shocked the world. The work drove vaccine rollout. Half a million young deaths a year, they found.
europmc-pmc3013263: Gender shapes health's causes and costs. This 2007 paper reviews how being male or female steers disease risks and outcomes. The author surveys the gaps worldwide. europmc-pmc3031263: Diabetes raises cancer risk; an old drug lowers it. This 2011 Taiwan study finds diabetics face more cancers, while metformin users face fewer. The authors' data intrigues cancer doctors. Their work spurred prevention trials. Liver and pancreas showed the biggest swings.
europmc-pmc6584763: Tumors are ecosystems, not just rogue cells - and math can model the whole show. europmc-pmc6603263: RSV is famous as a baby virus - but it hospitalizes and kills older adults too, sometimes rivaling flu. europmc-pmc6610963: Tumors rewire their metabolism to grow - and one overlooked detour, the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway, feeds their sugar-coating machinery. europmc-pmc6689963: Salmonella storms the gut with a molecular syringe - the type III secretion system encoded by pathogenicity island 1. europmc-pmc6704063: A tumor is a crowded neighborhood - cancer cells, immune cells, fibroblasts, each with its own metabolism. gao-gaoreports-gao-08-63: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report telling the State Department it needs transparent cost estimates to justify passport execution fees — the charges applicants pay when applying in person. gao-gaoreports-gao-07-863: Washington's wild lands were heating up in 2007 — GAO's report says federal land managers needed a real playbook for the changing climate. gao-gaoreports-gao-07-463: Anesthesia pay had a two-tier problem in 2007 — GAO's report compares what Medicare and private plans paid for putting patients under. The findings expose the payment gap. gao-gaoreports-gao-07-563: Charity status was shielding tax cheats in 2007 — GAO's report finds thousands of tax-exempt groups owed nearly a billion in payroll and other taxes. The findings strip the halo off the scofflaws. The report asks why the tax collector went soft on the nonprofit set.
openalex-w7206168763: Alzheimer's disease begins damaging the brain years before memory fails, so early detection matters enormously. openalex-w7204994563: The teacher's job is being reinvented by technology, and this article studies what that means for the profession. openalex-w7204254663: Bleeding after childbirth kills mothers, and every minute of delay matters. arxiv-2606-15963: Fine-tuning large AI models across many devices (federated learning) gets tricky when each device can only handle different-sized updates. PreLort nests smaller updates inside larger ones using a technique called LoRA, so every device contributes what it can. The paper presents the method and tests how well it trains models across mixed-capability devices.
arxiv-2606-16063: A theory paper about hard puzzles — like timetables and brain-teasers — where many rules must all hold at once. It looks at 'contested cluster selectors': spots where doubt close up forces long, costly back-tracking by solvers. The author works out the costs for random cases. For puzzle-theory experts.
arxiv-2606-16263: A fix-it note for an old wave-math paper. The first take made claims about wave rules (Schrödinger lines) that run for all time and split clean — and some lines need mending. The authors patch the text. Fix notes like this keep math frank.
arxiv-2606-16463: To morph one flat view to the next, math walks the curve-short path through flat-space (Grassmann turf). This paper paves two such walks: GLERP strides and loop-back GIDER strides. For pic-math pros who bend views true. Short walks save wobble and work.
arxiv-2606-16763: Local differential privacy adds noise on your device so companies can't identify you — but is it enough? This paper studies cross-silo de-anonymization: combining data from many sources to re-identify people despite the noise. It maps the threat and the tipping point where privacy breaks.
